content:
A common argument runs like this: look at the countries where Islam is the majority religion, and compare them to the West. Lower scores on human development, weaker protections for women, less press freedom, more authoritarian government. The pattern gets read as a verdict on the religion itself, as though Islam were the one variable that explains the gap.

The numbers behind the claim are frequently real. What is wrong is the inference drawn from them. Five facts below take the comparison seriously rather than dismissing it, and show what actually predicts the outcomes the claim points to.

Start with the honest version of the claim. In 2002 the United Nations Development Programme published the first Arab Human Development Report, written by a team of Arab researchers working under the Regional Bureau for Arab States rather than by outside critics.[1] It named three deficits holding the region back: a deficit of freedom, a deficit in the standing of women, and a deficit in knowledge production relative to income.[2] The report found Arab states scoring lowest on a composite freedom index among seven world regions surveyed, below sub-Saharan Africa.[3]

That report was not a one-off. The UNDP followed it with three more editions through 2005, each expanding on one of the three deficits in detail.[4] A reader who wants the index numbers does not need an outside polemicist. The strongest version of this argument has already been made, in more depth and with more data, by the people it describes. The report’s lead author, the Egyptian statistician Nader Fergany, directed the project under UNDP sponsorship and drew on teams of researchers based in universities across the Arab world, not on a single outside viewpoint.[5]

What the report does not do is hand the deficit to Islam as a religion. It names causes: entrenched single-party and monarchical rule, weak civil institutions, underinvestment in research, and restrictions on women’s legal and economic standing enforced by states, not by the Quran directly. The next four entries take each of those causes in turn.

The political scientist Michael Ross tested whether oil wealth itself, independent of any other factor, pushes a state away from democracy. His 2001 study in World Politics found a consistent negative relationship between a country’s dependence on oil exports and its level of democracy, holding across regions and not limited to the Middle East.[6] He identified three mechanisms: a taxation effect, where a government funded by resource rents has no need to tax citizens and so faces less pressure to represent them; a spending effect, where oil revenue buys political quiet through subsidies, public jobs, and patronage; and a repression effect, where the same revenue funds internal security forces strong enough to suppress dissent.[7]

None of those three mechanisms names a religion. They apply to Venezuela and Gabon as much as to Saudi Arabia, and research on the oil curse treats Brunei, a Muslim-majority sultanate, and non-Muslim Equatorial Guinea as the same kind of case.[8] A reader who wants to isolate Islam as a variable has to explain why the mechanism works identically in states with no Muslim population at all.

This does not clear every Gulf monarchy of its own record on rights and representation. It does mean the explanation on offer, that Islam itself produces authoritarian government, is competing against a simpler and better-tested one: a government that does not need its citizens’ money has less reason to answer to them, oil wealth being the clearest way to arrange that. Tunisia, a Muslim-majority state with negligible oil revenue, built the only durable multiparty transition to come out of the 2011 Arab uprisings, holding competitive elections and adopting a new constitution in 2014 before a later reversal under President Kais Saied; whatever explains that trajectory, it tracks the presence or absence of resource rents and institutional capacity far more closely than it tracks the country’s religion, which did not change at any point in the sequence.[9]

A large share of Muslim-majority states were still under direct or indirect European colonial administration deep into the twentieth century: Indonesia until 1949, most of the Arab Gulf states until the early 1970s, and Afghanistan was never formally colonised but absorbed the costs of repeated great-power proxy conflict instead.[10] Institutions built for extraction rather than self-government, the economists Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson argue, tend to persist well past the colonial period itself, shaping the political and economic path a country can take afterward regardless of what religion its population holds.[11]

Somalia is the sharpest illustration in the comparison this claim likes to draw. Its HDI value sits at 0.404, ranked 192nd of the countries the UNDP tracks, the third-lowest score recorded anywhere in the world.[12] The collapse driving that number traces to a specific and datable event: the fall of the Siad Barre government in 1991 and the state collapse that followed it, not to a religious tradition that predates that collapse by thirteen centuries and that Somalia shares with states that score nowhere near the bottom of the same index.[13]

Colonial timing is one input among several, not a single alternative explanation offered to replace religion with another monocausal story. It belongs in the same comparison as the oil-rent mechanism above: both predict the outcome without needing Islam as a variable, which is exactly why a claim that leans on Islam alone has to account for them.

Treat "Muslim-majority country" as a single category and the claim about backwardness needs that category to behave consistently. It does not. The UAE scores 0.940 on the UNDP’s Human Development Index, ranked 15th of the countries measured, ahead of France and Belgium. Qatar scores 0.886, ranked 43rd. Turkey scores 0.853, ranked 51st, and Malaysia scores 0.819, ranked 67th, all four in the index’s Very High development band.[14] Indonesia, the country with the largest Muslim population on earth, scores 0.728, ranked 113th, solidly in the High band.[15]

Set those against Afghanistan at 0.496, Yemen at 0.470, and Somalia at 0.404, the three lowest-ranked Muslim-majority states in the index.[16] The spread between the UAE’s rank of 15 and Somalia’s rank of 192 is larger than the spread between most pairs of countries anyone would call culturally unrelated. A single variable, shared identically by all eight of these states, cannot explain outcomes that differ this much between them.

What actually tracks the difference is closer to the two mechanisms already named: resource income paired with functioning state capacity in the UAE and Qatar, decades of comparatively stable governance and export-led growth in Malaysia and Turkey, against prolonged state collapse or civil war in Afghanistan, Yemen, and Somalia. Religion is the one factor held constant across all eight cases. It is also the one factor that explains none of the variance between them.

The complaint that Muslim societies fell behind a West they had once rivalled or surpassed is not new, and Muslims were not the last to raise it. The Egyptian reformer Muhammad Abduh, writing in the late nineteenth century, built an entire intellectual program, the Nahda or "awakening," around the question of why Muslim-majority societies had stagnated scientifically and politically while Christian Europe had not, arguing the fault lay in the ossification of religious institutions and legal interpretation rather than in Islam’s original sources.[17] That argument runs through more than a century of Muslim reformist writing since, not as an apologetic response to Western criticism but as an internal diagnosis that predates most of today’s online polemic by over 100 years. The Pakistani-American scholar Fazlur Rahman carried the same project into the twentieth century, arguing in his 1982 study Islam and Modernity that Muslim societies needed a revived method of legal and theological reasoning capable of engaging the modern world without treating either wholesale rejection or wholesale imitation of the West as the only options.[18]

The Arab Human Development Report picked up the same question in a different register in 2002, and it did not flinch from the parts of the record that are actually bad. It documented women excluded from large shares of formal political and economic life in specific named states, media environments with heavy state control, and research output far below what the region’s income level would predict elsewhere.[19] None of that gets minimised here. A government that restricts half its population’s legal standing is a real problem whatever the stated justification, and pretending otherwise would hand the honest version of this argument back to its critics.

What the internal record does not support is the leap from "some Muslim-majority states have serious, documented problems" to "Islam causes backwardness." The people closest to the problem, writing for more than a century before this argument became a comment-section talking point, have consistently located the causes somewhere more specific: colonial institutions, resource rents, authoritarian consolidation, and interpretive traditions within Islamic law that are themselves contested and have changed before. A single-variable verdict on the religion skips past all of that work to arrive at a conclusion the people who did the work did not reach.

The bottom line

The index numbers behind this claim are real, and the first people to publish them in detail were Arab researchers, not outside critics. What does not survive contact with the data is the single-cause story. Oil wealth predicts authoritarian government in Muslim and non-Muslim states alike. Colonial institutions left some Muslim-majority states with a harder starting position than others. And the category itself spans a United Arab Emirates ranked 15th in the world on human development and a Somalia ranked 192nd, a gap no single shared variable can explain.

None of this excuses the real record in specific states: restricted rights for women, state-controlled media, and authoritarian rule are documented problems, named as such by the Arab Human Development Report itself and by over a century of Muslim reformist writing before it. The honest version of this argument was made from inside the tradition it is accused of defending, and it reached a more specific, more useful diagnosis than "Islam is the cause."

Notes

  1. United Nations Development Programme, Regional Bureau for Arab States, Arab Human Development Report 2002: Creating Opportunities for Future Generations (New York: UNDP, 2002), prepared by a team of Arab researchers and intellectuals.
  2. Arab Human Development Report 2002, identifying deficits in freedom, women’s empowerment, and knowledge as the report’s three central findings.
  3. Arab Human Development Report 2002, on the region’s composite freedom index score relative to six other world regions surveyed in the report.
  4. United Nations Development Programme, Arab Human Development Report series, subsequent editions published in 2003 (knowledge), 2004 (freedom and governance), and 2005 (women’s empowerment).
  5. United Nations Development Programme, Arab Human Development Report 2002, directed by lead author Nader Fergany with contributing teams of researchers from universities across the Arab region.
  6. Michael L. Ross, "Does Oil Hinder Democracy?" World Politics 53, no. 3 (April 2001): 325–361.
  7. Ross, "Does Oil Hinder Democracy?" on the taxation, spending, and repression effects as the three mechanisms linking resource rents to reduced democratic pressure.
  8. Ross, "Does Oil Hinder Democracy?" testing the oil-democracy relationship across oil-exporting states generally, not limited to the Middle East or to Muslim-majority states; see also comparative treatments of Brunei and Equatorial Guinea as resource-rentier states with similarly weak democratic institutions despite differing state religions.
  9. On Tunisia’s 2014 constitution and its 2011–2021 multiparty transition, followed by President Kais Saied’s 2021 suspension of parliament and subsequent consolidation of power, see standard reference accounts of the Tunisian transition following the 2010–2011 uprising.
  10. On the end dates of colonial rule across Muslim-majority states (Indonesia’s independence recognised in 1949; the Gulf states’ British-administered treaty relationships ending between 1961 and 1971) and on Afghanistan’s history as a site of repeated great-power rivalry rather than formal colonisation, see standard reference histories of decolonisation in Asia and the Middle East.
  11. Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson, Why Nations Fail: The Origins of Power, Prosperity, and Poverty (New York: Crown Business, 2012), on the persistence of extractive colonial-era institutions as a predictor of later underdevelopment independent of a state’s religion or culture.
  12. United Nations Development Programme, Human Development Report, most recent country rankings, Somalia: HDI value 0.404, global rank 192 of 193 countries and territories ranked.
  13. On the 1991 collapse of the Siad Barre government and the subsequent Somali state collapse as the proximate cause of the country’s development indicators, see standard reference histories of the Somali Civil War.
  14. United Nations Development Programme, Human Development Report, most recent country rankings: United Arab Emirates, HDI value 0.940, global rank 15; Qatar, HDI value 0.886, global rank 43; Turkey, HDI value 0.853, global rank 51; Malaysia, HDI value 0.819, global rank 67; all four classified in the Very High human development band (HDI of 0.800 or above).
  15. United Nations Development Programme, Human Development Report, most recent country rankings: Indonesia, HDI value 0.728, global rank 113, in the High human development band.
  16. United Nations Development Programme, Human Development Report, most recent country rankings: Afghanistan, HDI value 0.496, global rank 181; Yemen, HDI value 0.470, global rank 184; Somalia, HDI value 0.404, global rank 192; all three in the Low human development band.
  17. Fazlur Rahman, Islam and Modernity: Transformation of an Intellectual Tradition (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1982).
  18. On Muhammad Abduh (1849–1905) and the Nahda reform movement’s diagnosis of Muslim civilizational decline as rooted in the ossification of legal and religious institutions rather than in Islam’s original sources, see standard intellectual histories of Islamic modernism, e.g. Albert Hourani, Arabic Thought in the Liberal Age, 1798–1939 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1962; repr. 1983).
  19. Arab Human Development Report 2002, on women’s exclusion from formal political and economic participation, state control of media, and research and development spending as a share of GDP across the surveyed states.
